column2: Information retrieval systems use inverted indexes for efficient search
The vector space model represents documents and queries as vectors
Boolean retrieval uses AND OR and NOT operators
TF IDF measures the importance of terms in documents
Search engines rank documents according to their relevance
BM25 is a ranking function used in information retrieval
Neural information retrieval uses deep learning models
Dense retrieval represents queries and documents using embeddings
Vector databases support similarity search over embeddings
Search engines use inverted indexes to retrieve documents efficiently
An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it
The Boolean model returns documents that exactly match the query expression
Cosine similarity compares the angle between a query vector and a document vector
BM25 improves TF IDF with term frequency saturation and document length normalization
Dense retrieval encodes documents into embeddings and searches nearest neighbors
Indexation builds data structures that speed up information retrieval
Information retrieval evaluates the relevance of documents for a user query
Inverse document frequency gives higher weight to rare terms in the collection
The vector model ranks documents by similarity with the query unlike the Boolean model
Web search engines crawl pages then build an index for fast retrieval
Term frequency counts how many times a term occurs in a document
Embeddings capture semantic similarity between words queries and documents
Query processing in search engines uses tokenization stopword removal and stemming
Hybrid search combines BM25 and dense retrieval to improve ranking quality
Precision and recall are metrics used to evaluate retrieval models
